make: verb
produce or create something
typical: make + noun: a cake, a table, a noise. NOT for: forcing (see make sb do).
She makes great soup.
They made a table from old wood.
verb
prepare food or drink
typical: make coffee/dinner/a sandwich. NOT for: buying ready-made food.
I'll make some tea.
He made lunch for everyone.
verb
do an action expressed by the noun
typical: make a decision/call/mistake/plan/suggestion. NOT for: housework (use do).
I need to make a phone call.
He made a mistake.
verb
force or cause someone to do or feel something
typical: make + person + verb/adjective. NOT for: allowing.
The film made me cry.
Her boss made her redo the report.
verb
succeed in getting somewhere in time, or succeed in general
typical: make it. NOT for: producing things.
We just made it to the airport.
I can't make it to the meeting tonight.
make do: manage with what you have although it is not ideal
typical: make do (with sth), make do without. NOT for: getting what you want.
We have to make do with a small flat.
There's no milk, so we'll make do.
make for: go in the direction of a place
typical: make for home/the exit. NOT for: leaving it.
I think it's time we made for home.
cause or help to produce a result
typical: make for a great game/good results. NOT for: preventing.
Both teams are on good form, which should make for a great game.
Short meetings make for better work.
make fun of: laugh at someone in an unkind way
typical: make fun of sb/sth. NOT for: praising.
The other kids make fun of his accent.
make into: change something into a different form or purpose
typical: make sth into sth. NOT for: keeping it.
We can make your room into a study.
They made the barn into a house.
typical: make sb into sth. NOT for: leaving unchanged.
The film made her into a star overnight.
Fame made him into a monster.
make off: typical: make off (with sth). NOT for: staying.
The men made off as police arrived.
A car made off down the road.
make out: verb
just manage to see or hear something
typical: make sth out, can't make out what he said. NOT for: understanding reasons.
I could just make out a dark shape.
I couldn't make out what he was saying.
verb
understand something, especially why it happened
typical: make out what/how/why. NOT for: seeing something.
I can't make out why she left.
As far as I can make out, he is not married.
verb
understand someone's character and behaviour
typical: can't make sb out. NOT for: hearing something.
Stuart is a strange guy - I can't make him out.
I can't make my boss out at all.
verb
write something such as a cheque, list or bill
typical: make out a cheque/list/will. NOT for: understanding.
She was making out a list of guests.
Make the cheque out to 'Grays Ltd'.
verb
say that something is true when it is not
typical: make out (that) ..., make sb out to be sth. NOT for: telling the truth.
He makes me out to be an idiot.
She made out that she was ill.
verb
find good reasons to support an idea or request
typical: make out a case for sth. NOT for: pretending.
We made out a case for hiring another assistant.
He made out a strong case for change.
verb
manage or succeed in a particular way (especially AmE)
typical: how did you make out?. NOT for: seeing or hearing.
How did you make out at the interview?
She made out fine in her new job.
make over: officially give money or property to someone else
typical: make sth over (to sb). NOT for: keeping.
He made over the estate to his son.
She made her house over to her sister.
change someone or something so it looks different or has a new use
typical: make sb/sth over. NOT for: keeping the same.
She made herself over for the film role.
make up: verb
combine to form something; be the parts of something
typical: be made up of sth, make up a part/percentage. NOT for: inventing something.
Women make up a small part of the group.
The team is made up of ten students.
verb
invent a story, excuse or lie
typical: make up a story/excuse/lie, make sth up. NOT for: forming a group.
I think they're making the whole thing up.
He made up an excuse for being late.
verb
create something new by thinking, such as a song or a game
typical: make up a song/game/rules. NOT for: telling lies.
Nick made up a song about them.
The children made up a new game.
verb
prepare something by mixing or putting parts together
typical: make up a bed/a bottle/a prescription. NOT for: inventing.
Can you make up a bed on the sofa?
The pharmacist made up the medicine.
verb
put make-up on someone's face
typical: be made up, make sb up. NOT for: putting make-up on yourself.
They made him up as an old man.
The actress was made up for the scene.
verb
add to an amount to reach the level needed
typical: make up the rest/difference. NOT for: forming parts of a whole.
My parents made up the rest of the money.
Who will make up the difference?
verb
become friends again after a quarrel
typical: make up with sb, kiss and make up. NOT for: inventing.
They argued but soon made up.
She made up with her sister.
make up for: make a bad situation better or replace what was lost
typical: make up for sth, make up for lost time. NOT for: worsening.
The team will want to make up for a poor start.
I don't eat breakfast but I make up for it at lunch.
have so much of one quality that a lack of another does not matter
typical: sth makes up for sth. NOT for: lacking both.
His enthusiasm makes up for his lack of skill.
Her charm makes up for it.
mark down: typical: mark sth down (by sth). NOT for: raising prices.
All coats are marked down by 30%.
The shop marked down winter stock.
give a lower score to a student or piece of work
typical: mark sb/sth down. NOT for: marking up.
The teacher marked me down for spelling.
He was marked down for late work.
consider someone to be a particular type (BrE)
typical: mark sb down as sth. NOT for: ignoring.
I marked him down as a future star.
They marked her down as a troublemaker.
mark up: increase the price of something so you can make a profit
typical: mark sth up (by sth). NOT for: reducing prices.
write notes or corrections on a document
typical: mark sth up. NOT for: leaving clean.
The editor marked up the text.
mean: have or express a particular meaning
typical: mean + noun/clause; word or sign + mean. NOT for: intention.
say something with a particular intention (often to check understanding)
typical: what you mean / do you mean / if you know what I mean. NOT for: word meanings in a dictionary sense.
Do you mean you've changed your mind?
typical: mean to + verb. NOT for: word meanings.
I didn't mean to upset you.
She meant to call you yesterday.
meanwhile: says that something else is happening during the same time
typical: neutral, at the start of a sentence. NOT for: 'later' (use 'afterwards').
Prepare the sauce. Meanwhile, boil the pasta.
He was shopping; meanwhile, the children were at school.
The talks continue. Meanwhile, prices keep rising.
meet: verb
see someone by arrangement
typical: meet + person, meet at + place/time. NOT for: chance encounters.
Let's meet at the cafe at eight.
I'll meet you outside the theatre.
verb
see someone by chance
typical: meet + person unexpectedly. NOT for: planned meetings.
I met an old friend in the street.
You'll never guess who I met on the bus.
verb
see and talk to someone for the first time
typical: nice/pleased to meet you, meet + new person. NOT for: seeing again.
I met my husband at university.
Nice to meet you.
verb
wait for someone at an airport, station or stop
typical: meet + person at the airport/station. NOT for: general meetings.
I'll meet you off the plane.
Can you meet her at the station?
verb
come together for a discussion or event
typical: the committee/team/group meets, meet to discuss. NOT for: two people greeting.
The committee meets once a month.
The two groups will meet next week.
verb
satisfy a need, demand, requirement or standard
typical: meet requirements/needs/demands/standards. NOT for: people.
The product meets all safety rules.
The school tries to meet the needs of every child.
verb
reach or achieve a deadline or target
typical: meet a deadline/target/goal. NOT for: people.
We must meet the deadline.
The company met its sales targets.
verb
join or touch at a point (of roads, lines or rivers)
typical: roads/lines/rivers meet. NOT for: people.
The two roads meet near the village.
The river meets the sea here.
mess around: verb
spend time lazily, doing things slowly without a plan (informal)
typical: mess around (on sth), mess about (BrE). NOT for: working hard.
He spent his holiday messing around on the farm.
We just messed around at home.
verb
behave in a silly way when you should be serious
typical: mess around, Stop messing around!. NOT for: paying attention.
Stop messing around and get ready for school.
The kids were messing around in class.
verb
cause problems for someone, especially by changing plans (BrE)
typical: mess sb around. NOT for: being clear.
The airline messed us around.
Don't mess me around.
verb
touch or play with something carelessly
typical: mess around with sth. NOT for: using properly.
Don't mess around with the wires.
He messed around with my phone.
mess up: verb
spoil or ruin something, especially something important
typical: mess sth up. NOT for: improving.
I don't want some idiot to mess it up.
She felt she'd messed up her whole life.
verb
make something dirty or untidy
typical: mess sth up. NOT for: tidying.
Who messed up the kitchen?
The wind messed up my hair.
verb
make a mistake and do something badly
typical: mess up (sth). NOT for: succeeding.
I think I messed up the interview.
He messed up and lost his job.
verb
cause someone serious emotional problems, or injure them badly (informal)
typical: mess sb up, be messed up. NOT for: helping.
His parents' divorce really messed him up.
The crash messed her up badly.
miss out: not have the chance to do something you would enjoy
typical: miss out (on sth). NOT for: taking part.
Some children miss out because their parents can't pay.
Don't miss out on the fun!
typical: miss sb/sth out. NOT for: including.
Make sure you don't miss any details out.
She missed out the last paragraph.
mix up: verb
think a person or thing is another one by mistake
typical: mix sb/sth up (with sb/sth). NOT for: telling apart.
I always mix him up with his brother.
I must have got the times mixed up.
verb
change the order of things so they are no longer arranged
typical: mix sth up. NOT for: sorting.
Someone has mixed up my papers.
The cards got mixed up.
verb
make someone confused (be mixed up)
typical: be mixed up. NOT for: being clear.
I'm all mixed up about it.
She felt mixed up.
verb
be involved in something bad (be mixed up in sth)
typical: be mixed up in/with sth. NOT for: staying out.
He got mixed up in a fraud.
She is mixed up with criminals.
mop up: remove liquid with a mop or cloth
typical: mop sth up. NOT for: spilling.
Mop the sauce up with your bread.
He mopped up the spilt milk.
deal with what remains of a problem or enemy
typical: mop up opposition/the rest. NOT for: starting.
Soldiers were sent to mop up resistance.
They mopped up the last of the work.
more specifically: gives more exact detail about what you have just said
typical: neutral to formal, after a general statement. NOT for: introducing a new topic.
I work in IT, more specifically in cyber security.
We need help, more specifically with design.
The problem is technical. More specifically, it is a software error.
moreover: adds an extra point that strengthens the argument
typical: formal, written, at the start of a sentence. NOT for: contrast (use 'however').
The idea is cheap. Moreover, it is easy to test.
The hotel is clean; moreover, the staff are friendly.
He is experienced and, moreover, very honest.
move away: go to live in a different area
typical: move away (from + place). NOT for: moving in.
My best friend moved away when I was ten.
They moved away from the city.
go further from someone or something
typical: move away (from sb/sth). NOT for: approaching.
He moved away from the window.
move in: verb
start living in a new home
typical: move in, move into sth, move in on Monday. NOT for: leaving a home.
When are you moving in?
They moved into a smaller house.
verb
start living with someone in the same home
typical: move in with sb. NOT for: living alone.
Steve is moving in with her.
They moved in together last year.
verb
start to get involved in and control something others controlled
typical: big firms/investors move in (on sth). NOT for: leaving a place.
Big firms moved in and raised prices.
Investors moved in on the market.
verb
go towards a place or people to attack or take control
typical: move in on sb/sth. NOT for: moving house.
Police moved in on the demonstrators.
Troops moved in on the city.
move on: leave one place and go to another
typical: move on to the next town, move on. NOT for: staying.
After a week we moved on to the next village.
The police told the crowd to move on.
start a new activity or topic
typical: move on to sth. NOT for: continuing the same topic.
Let's move on to the next question.
After lunch we moved on to the second chapter.
stop thinking about the past and start a new stage of life
typical: move on with your life. NOT for: staying in the past.
It is time to forget him and move on.
She found a new job and moved on.
move out: leave the home where you live to live somewhere else
typical: move out, move out of + place. NOT for: moving in.
He moved out and they divorced a year later.
They moved out of London when he was little.
leave a place (soldiers) or leave (AmE spoken)
typical: troops move out, ready to move out?. NOT for: moving into a place.
The troops moved out at dawn.
Are you ready to move out?
move over: verb
change your position to make room for someone
typical: move over (a little). NOT for: staying.
Move over a little so I can get in.
Move over, please.
verb
start using a different system or doing different work
typical: move over (to sth). NOT for: staying.
Most firms have moved over to computers.
The school moved over to a new method.
verb
change jobs, especially within the same field
typical: move over (from sth). NOT for: staying.
The new publisher moved over from another company.
She moved over to the BBC.
verb
used humorously to say that something new is becoming more popular than something older
typical: Move over + name/thing. NOT for: praising the old.
Move over, vinyl: streaming is here.
Move over, CDs!
muddle through: succeed in doing something with difficulty or not very well
typical: muddle through (sth). NOT for: planning well.
I managed to muddle through the questions.
The team muddled through another season.
